items.purpose: The programme brief is the one-page introduction to Project Beacon. It tells a newcomer what problem Beacon solves, what the three releases deliver, who is involved, how success is measured, what it costs and what could go wrong. You, the Programme Manager, write it in week 1, day 1 and refresh it whenever the numbers change. Dr. Helen Marchetti, the executive sponsor, approves it. Leaders, clinicians, vendors and new team members read it before their first Beacon meeting, and you reuse its wording in the business case, the charter and every status report.

sections.heading: The problem in numbers
sections.guidance: Describe Beacon's three problems (untrusted patient-flow numbers, slow and unsafe access, untested recovery) as facts a reader can check. Give each one or two baseline figures and the period they cover. Skip adjectives such as poor or broken and let the numbers make the point. It is good when someone who has never worked at Kestrel can say what is wrong, and how bad it is, after 30 seconds, and every number matches the Q3 2026 baseline as of 2026-10-01.

sections.heading: What Beacon delivers
sections.guidance: Show the three releases in one table: the release, what it delivers in outcome language, and its gate date. Say that Beacon has one charter, one budget, one schedule and one change-control board, because that is what makes it a programme rather than three projects. Judge it by whether a charge nurse could tell which release changes their work, and when.

sections.heading: Who is involved
sections.guidance: List only the people a newcomer needs: the sponsor, the change-control board chair, the privacy and security owners, the service owner, the data owners and you. Give the name, employee ID and what each person decides. A good list tells the reader who to go to for which decision. It is not an organization chart.

sections.heading: How success is measured
sections.guidance: Copy the nine charter measures with the baseline from data and the target agreed with the sponsor, and say when they are measured (three months after each release). Label baselines as data and targets as agreed. It is good when every measure is a number someone else can recompute and none of them is a task such as build a dashboard.

sections.heading: Budget and timeline
sections.guidance: State the budget at completion, the management reserve, total authorized funding, the start and finish dates and the gate dates, plus one honest line on the current cost and schedule position. Define each earned value term the first time you use it. Judge it by whether the sponsor would see exactly the same numbers in the charter and the status report.

sections.heading: Top risks and open issues
sections.guidance: Pick the four or five risks a newcomer must know, with ID and owner, and list the open issues. Point to the RAID log for the rest. Good: short, every line owned, and the IDs match the RAID log exactly.

sections.heading: How Beacon is run
sections.guidance: In a few bullets, explain how decisions are made and recorded, where change requests go, how sensitive information is handled and how often people hear from you. Good: a new team member knows what to do with a change request or a privacy question on their first day.

## The problem in numbers

Kestrel Health Network (KHN) runs Kestrel General Hospital (KGH), Aspen Ridge Hospital (ARH), Coulee Valley Hospital (CVH) and Prairie Gate Health Centre (PGH). Three problems put patients and their information at risk.

1. Patient-flow leaders work from Excel extracts emailed every morning. Sites count differently, nobody trusts the numbers, and the extracts carry more patient detail than anyone needs. At KGH the median time from arrival to physician initial assessment (PIA) was 80.5 minutes, and 7.5% of emergency department (ED) visits left without being seen (LWBS), against 5.7% across all sites.
2. Clinicians wait days for access and some people keep it after they leave. In the service desk extract (August and September 2026) the median access request took 4.26 days and only 27.3% were resolved within 72 hours. Two workers who had left still had enabled accounts, 2 of 6 privileged accounts had no multi-factor authentication (MFA), and one administrator held provision, approve and audit-log rights on the Identity Directory.
3. Kestrel cannot show it could keep caring for patients through a ransomware attack. Both restore tests of the Clinical Information System (CIS, A-001) missed its 4-hour recovery time objective (RTO), at 9.0 and 13.5 hours. The last test was on 2025-08-14, 413 days before 2026-10-01.

## What Beacon delivers

One programme, one charter, one budget, one schedule and one change-control board (CCB), from 2026-09-01 to 2026-12-17.

| Release | What it delivers | Gate |
|---|---|---|
| 1 Patient-flow analytics service | Power BI dashboards for ED flow and bed occupancy on de-identified, aggregated data, secured by site with row-level security (RLS), supported by the service desk | Go-live 2026-10-23 |
| 2 Clinician identity and access | Access driven by human resources (HR) joiner-mover-leaver events and roles, MFA and single sign-on, privileged access control, quarterly access reviews, access requests as a measured service | Acceptance 2026-11-26 |
| 3 Cyber resilience | Business impact analysis, recovery targets, a tested CIS restore and downtime procedures, incident response, vulnerability remediation, a security-operations dashboard, programme closure | Programme acceptance 2026-12-17 |

## Who is involved

- Dr. Helen Marchetti (E-001), executive sponsor: owns the business case, holds the management reserve, decides the gates.
- Marcus Bell (E-002), Chief Information Officer: chairs the CCB.
- Priya Raman (E-003), Chief Privacy Officer: approves the privacy impact assessment.
- Daniel Osei (E-004), Chief Information Security Officer: security owner and risk acceptance advisor.
- Grace Liu (E-005), IT Service Desk Manager: service owner of the analytics service, which her service desk supports.
- Tomás Rivera (E-006), Clinical Analytics Lead: builds the semantic model, data steward.
- Dr. Sarah Whitford (E-007) owns emergency data. Janelle Cardinal (E-008) owns bed data and is the main dashboard user.
- Programme Manager: runs the plan, the RAID (risks, assumptions, issues and decisions) log and reporting.

## How success is measured

Baselines are Kestrel data. Targets are agreed with the sponsor and measured three months after each gate: Release 1 measures on 2027-01-25, Release 2 measures on 2027-02-26, and Release 3 and programme measures on 2027-03-17.

| Measure | Baseline (data) | Target (agreed) |
|---|---|---|
| Median minutes, arrival to PIA, KGH | 80.5 | 60 |
| LWBS rate, all sites | 5.7% | 4.5% |
| Access requests resolved within 72 hours | 27.3% | 80% |
| Median days to fulfil an access request | 4.26 | 1 |
| Missed leavers (accounts enabled after the worker left) | 2 | 0 |
| Privileged accounts with MFA | 66.7% | 100% |
| Q3 access reviews completed on time | 66.7% | 100% |
| CIS restore within its 4-hour RTO | Failed (9.0 h and 13.5 h) | Pass |
| Security awareness, agency and vendor workers | 48% | 90% |

## Budget and timeline

- Budget at completion (BAC): CAD (Canadian dollars) 1,200,000 across 15 work packages. Release 1 CAD 420,000, Release 2 CAD 460,000, Release 3 CAD 320,000.
- Management reserve (agreed, held by the sponsor): CAD 120,000. Total authorized: CAD 1,320,000.
- 78 working days, Monday to Friday. Gates on 2026-10-23, 2026-11-26 and 2026-12-17.
- Position on 2026-10-01: earned value (EV) CAD 224,000 against planned value (PV) CAD 278,900 and actual cost (AC) CAD 250,600. Cost performance index (CPI) 0.89 and schedule performance index (SPI) 0.80: behind plan and over cost.

## Top risks and open issues

- R-01 ED extract data quality undermines trust in the dashboards. Owner: Tomás Rivera.
- R-02 Small counts at PGH (55 valid visits in Q3) could identify patients. Owner: Priya Raman.
- R-04 The CIS cannot be restored within its 4-hour RTO. Owner: Daniel Osei.
- R-08 Cost performance could exhaust the management reserve. Owner: Marcus Bell.
- Open issues: I-01 Kevin Park (E-009) holds provision, approve and audit-log rights; I-02 missed leavers E-014 and E-027 still enabled; I-03 CIS restore tests failed twice.

All eight risks (R-01 to R-08) are in the RAID log, BCN-R1-11.

## How Beacon is run

- Every decision gets an ID in the RAID log. D-01: charter approved by Dr. Helen Marchetti on 2026-09-01.
- Changes to scope, gate dates or budget go to the CCB before any baseline moves.
- Dashboards are classified Confidential. Kestrel policy suppresses any count under 5, and blanks any rate whose numerator is under 5, in any report shared outside the care team.
- The sponsor gets a weekly status report. Documents are numbered BCN-R1, BCN-R2 and BCN-R3 by release.
mistakes: Leading with tasks and technology. Leaders read the brief to decide whether Beacon matters to them, so open with the three problems and their numbers.
Quoting figures without a period or a source. Every number in the brief is the Q3 2026 baseline as of 2026-10-01, and a reader should be able to find it in the data.
Presenting agreed targets as results. 60 minutes and 4.5% are targets the sponsor agreed, not achievements, so label them.
Shortening privacy impact assessment to initials. Beacon reserves those initials for physician initial assessment, so write the privacy document's name in full every time.

items.purpose: The coverage map links every exam objective you must pass to the Beacon document and the session where you practise it: all 26 PMP tasks, the four PL-300 skill areas, the eight CISSP domains and the ITIL Foundation (Version 5) topics. You write it in week 1, day 2 and own it. There is no outside approver, though a study partner or mentor can review it. You use it to see where coverage is thin, to plan revision before each exam gate, and to confirm every objective has been practised before you sit.

sections.heading: How to read the map
sections.guidance: Explain the session code (W2 D3 means week 2, day 3), what one row means, and where the documents live (Project). Copy each objective name exactly as the publisher words it, so you learn the wording the exam uses. Good: anyone can find the session and document for an objective in a few seconds.

sections.heading: PMP: People (33%)
sections.guidance: List all eight People tasks with their number and exact name, then the Beacon document and session where you practise each one. People tasks are about vision, conflict, leadership, stakeholders, knowledge transfer and communication, so they map to the brief, the charter, the stakeholder register, the communication plan, the team charter and change control. Good: every task has a session, and the conflict and team tasks point to week 9, where a real Beacon conflict happens.

sections.heading: PMP: Process (41%)
sections.guidance: List all ten Process tasks. These are planning and control tasks, so they map to scope, WBS, schedule, quality, cost, procurement, earned value and closure documents. Process is the heaviest domain, so check that most tasks appear twice: once when you plan and once when you control or close.

sections.heading: PMP: Business Environment (26%)
sections.guidance: List all eight Business Environment tasks: governance, compliance, change, issues, risk, continuous improvement, organizational change and external change. Map them to the charter, change control, the privacy impact assessment, the RAID log and the improvement registers. Good: the external-change task names a real Beacon trigger, such as the ransomware attack at another hospital that led to Release 3.

sections.heading: PL-300 skill areas
sections.guidance: Give the four skill areas with their weights and, under each, the skill groups the study guide lists. Map them to the Power Query workbook, star schema, DAX catalogue, reports, RLS test pack and workspace plan. Most PL-300 practice sits in weeks 1 to 5, and the Release 2 and 3 dashboards keep it fresh. Good: no skill group depends only on a session after the week 6 gate.

sections.heading: CISSP domains
sections.guidance: List all eight domains with their weights and the Beacon documents that exercise each one. Release 1 covers classification, privacy and threat modelling, Release 2 identity and access, Release 3 operations and recovery. Good: each domain has at least one document you build yourself, not only one you read.

sections.heading: ITIL Foundation (Version 5) topics
sections.guidance: List the learning objectives: product and service management concepts, value co-creation, the four dimensions, the ITIL Value System, the seven guiding principles, the eight-stage product and service lifecycle, management practices, continual improvement and value stream mapping. Use Version 5 terms only. Good: every topic is practised before week 6, day 4, because ITIL is examined then.

sections.heading: Gates, gaps and review
sections.guidance: Name the three exam gates, call out the objectives with the thinnest coverage and say how you will repair them. Summarize the five readiness checks on Progress so ready has a fixed meaning. Good: you can point to the day on which each thin area gets extra practice.

items.purpose: The business case explains why Kestrel should spend money and people on Beacon. It compares realistic options, states the benefits with baselines, targets and owners, sets out costs and risks, and recommends one option. You write it for the executive sponsor in week 1, day 4. Dr. Helen Marchetti owns it and accepted it with the charter on 2026-09-01 (D-01). The CIO, the Chief Privacy Officer and the CISO review it. It is checked again at every gate, and at closure the programme closure report compares outcomes against it.

sections.heading: Problem and opportunity
sections.guidance: State each problem with its evidence and its consequence for patients, privacy or resilience. Use the Q3 baseline figures, not impressions. Finish with the opportunity: what becomes possible if the problems are solved together. Good: the sponsor could read this section aloud to the board and every number would hold up.

sections.heading: Options considered
sections.guidance: Compare at least three real options, including doing nothing and doing part of the work. For each, say what it delivers, what it costs, and what it leaves unsolved. Cost every option from the same estimates so the comparison is fair. Good: a reader can see why the rejected options fail, not just that they were rejected.

sections.heading: Benefits and measures
sections.guidance: Turn each outcome into a measure with a baseline from data, a target agreed with the sponsor, a benefit owner in the business and a date it is measured. Separate outputs (a dashboard) from benefits (fewer patients leaving unseen). Claim only benefits you can measure; if there is no reliable money figure, say so instead of inventing one.

sections.heading: Costs and funding
sections.guidance: Show the budget by release, the budget at completion, the management reserve and total authorized funding. When you refresh the case, add the current earned value position and the forecast at completion. Good: the numbers match the charter and the work package register exactly, and any forecast overrun is stated plainly.

sections.heading: Risks
sections.guidance: List the main risks of the recommended option with their RAID IDs and owners, and the main risk of doing nothing. Keep it short; the RAID log holds the detail. Good: the sponsor sees the risks she is accepting by approving, and who manages each one.

sections.heading: Privacy, security and service value
sections.guidance: Show how the option meets Kestrel's duties as a custodian under the Health Information Act, why the security case is a matter of due care, and how each release ends as a supported service that keeps creating value after go-live. Good: the privacy and security owners would sign this section without edits.

sections.heading: Recommendation and decision
sections.guidance: Recommend one option, say exactly what decision you need and from whom, and record the decision with its ID and date once made. On a refresh, say whether the recommendation still stands. Good: one clear ask, not a menu.

## Problem and opportunity

- Emergency department (ED) flow. Leaders decide from Excel extracts emailed each morning; sites disagree and the extracts hold more patient detail than needed. At Kestrel General Hospital (KGH) the median time from arrival to physician initial assessment (PIA) was 80.5 minutes. Across all sites only 28.3% of visits (126 of 445) were assessed within their Canadian Triage and Acuity Scale (CTAS) objective, and 5.7% left without being seen (LWBS).
- Clinician access. Access requests took a median 4.26 days, 27.3% were resolved within 72 hours and 15.2% met their service level. Two leavers kept enabled accounts, 2 of 6 privileged accounts lacked multi-factor authentication (MFA), and one administrator held provision, approve and audit-log rights.
- Cyber resilience. The Clinical Information System (CIS) missed its 4-hour recovery time objective (RTO) in both restore tests, at 9.0 and 13.5 hours, and has not been tested since 2025-08-14. After a ransomware attack at another hospital the board asked whether care could continue without clinical systems. Kestrel cannot yet show that it could.

Opportunity: the three problems share data, people and governance, so one programme can fix them by 2026-12-17.

## Options considered

Costs, in Canadian dollars (CAD), come from the 15 work-package estimates.

| Option | Delivers | Cost (CAD) | Assessment |
|---|---|---|---|
| A Do nothing | Extracts, manual access and untested restores continue | 0 | Rejected: every problem stays, and the extracts conflict with the duty to use the least information needed |
| B Analytics only | Release 1 | 420,000 | Rejected: leaves the missed leavers open, and leaves the CIS restore gap the board asked about |
| C Analytics and access | Releases 1 and 2 | 880,000 | Rejected: Kestrel still cannot show it can recover the CIS |
| D Full programme | Releases 1, 2 and 3 under one charter | 1,200,000 plus 120,000 reserve | Recommended |

Three separate projects were also considered and not costed: they need the same specialists under three governance structures.

## Benefits and measures

Beacon delivers the tools; each benefit comes when the business changes how it works with them. Baselines are data, targets are agreed with the sponsor, and each is measured three months after its gate: Release 1 measures on 2027-01-25, Release 2 measures on 2027-02-26, and Release 3 and programme measures on 2027-03-17.

| Measure | Baseline (data) | Target (agreed) | Benefit owner |
|---|---|---|---|
| Median minutes, arrival to PIA, KGH | 80.5 | 60 | Dr. Sarah Whitford (E-007) |
| LWBS rate, all sites | 5.7% | 4.5% | Dr. Sarah Whitford (E-007) |
| Access requests resolved within 72 hours | 27.3% | 80% | Grace Liu (E-005) |
| Median days to fulfil an access request | 4.26 | 1 | Grace Liu (E-005) |
| Missed leavers | 2 | 0 | Nora Lindqvist (E-018) |
| Privileged accounts with MFA | 66.7% | 100% | Daniel Osei (E-004) |
| Q3 access reviews completed on time | 66.7% | 100% | Daniel Osei (E-004) |
| CIS restore within its 4-hour RTO | Failed (9.0 h and 13.5 h) | Pass | Daniel Osei (E-004) |
| Security awareness, agency and vendor workers | 48% | 90% | Daniel Osei (E-004) |

The case claims no cash savings. Kestrel has no reliable cost data for waits or downtime, so it rests on measured service and risk outcomes.

## Costs and funding

| Item | CAD |
|---|---|
| Release 1 (WP-101 to WP-105) | 420,000 |
| Release 2 (WP-106 to WP-110) | 460,000 |
| Release 3 (WP-111 to WP-115) | 320,000 |
| Budget at completion (BAC) | 1,200,000 |
| Management reserve (agreed, held by the sponsor) | 120,000 |
| Total authorized | 1,320,000 |

Position on 2026-10-01: planned value CAD 278,900, earned value CAD 224,000, actual cost CAD 250,600. Cost performance index (CPI) 0.89 and schedule performance index 0.80. At this CPI the estimate at completion is CAD 1,342,500, a variance at completion of CAD -142,500. That is CAD 22,500 more than total authorized funding, so the reserve alone cannot absorb it (R-08).

## Risks

- Option D: R-01 ED data quality (Tomás Rivera, E-006); R-02 small counts at Prairie Gate Health Centre (Priya Raman, E-003); R-03 MFA slows clinicians at shared workstations (Janelle Cardinal, E-008); R-04 CIS restore misses its RTO (Daniel Osei, E-004); R-05 security logs processed in the United States (Priya Raman); R-06 key-person dependency on Tomás Rivera and R-07 Lumen Analytics Partners contract ends 2026-11-30 (Programme Manager); R-08 cost overrun (Marcus Bell, E-002).
- Option A: a ransomware attack would find a CIS that has never been restored within its RTO.

## Privacy, security and service value

- Privacy: the Health Information Act requires the highest degree of anonymity possible and only the amount of health information essential for the purpose (sections 57 and 58). De-identified, aggregated dashboards meet that; daily patient-level extracts do not. A privacy impact assessment goes to the Information and Privacy Commissioner for review and comment before go-live (section 64).
- Security: knowing the CIS restore fails and taking no action falls short of due care for a custodian of health information (section 60 safeguards).
- Service value: each release ends as a supported service with a named owner, so value keeps being co-created with clinicians after go-live. Every release must move at least one measure above.

## Recommendation and decision

Recommend option D. Decision D-01: accepted with the charter by Dr. Helen Marchetti on 2026-09-01. This refresh keeps option D and asks the change-control board for a cost recovery plan before any management reserve is released.
mistakes: Comparing only doing the project with doing nothing. Real options include doing part of the work; show what each one leaves unsolved and cost them from the same estimates.
Inventing savings. Kestrel has no reliable money figure for waits or downtime, so the case rests on measured patient-flow, access and recovery outcomes.
Listing outputs as benefits. A dashboard is an output; a lower LWBS rate with a baseline, target, owner and date is a benefit.
Filing it and forgetting it. Refresh the case at each gate: on 2026-10-01 the estimate at completion already exceeds total authorized funding.

items.purpose: The programme charter formally authorizes Project Beacon. It names the sponsor and the Programme Manager, gives the Programme Manager authority to use Kestrel resources, and fixes the objectives, high-level scope, milestones, budget, governance, privacy and security success criteria, and key risks. You draft it in week 1, day 5 from the business case; Dr. Helen Marchetti signs it (D-01, 2026-09-01). Every later plan, change request and gate decision is tested against it, and it changes only through the change-control board and the sponsor.

sections.heading: Purpose and justification
sections.guidance: In two or three sentences, say why Beacon exists and point to the business case for the evidence. Do not repeat the whole case. Good: a reader understands the reason for the programme without opening another document, and knows where the detail lives.

sections.heading: Objectives and success measures
sections.guidance: Write one objective per release in outcome language, then the success measures: baseline from data, target agreed with the sponsor, owner, and when measured. Each objective should be specific and time-bound. Good: at closure, someone can say yes or no to each measure without arguing about definitions.

sections.heading: High-level scope
sections.guidance: Say what each release includes at a summary level and, just as important, what is out of scope. Exclusions written here stop scope creep later and give the change-control board something firm to test requests against. Good: the scope statement and WBS can be traced back to these lines.

sections.heading: Milestones and budget
sections.guidance: List the summary milestones with dates and who decides each gate, then the budget at completion by release, the management reserve and who holds it, and total authorized funding. Good: the dates match the schedule and the money matches the register to the dollar.

sections.heading: Governance and authority
sections.guidance: Name the sponsor, the change-control board chair, the privacy, security and service owners, and the data owners, and say what each decides. State the Programme Manager's authority plainly: what you may decide alone and what must go to the board or the sponsor. Good: no decision in Beacon has two possible owners or none.

sections.heading: Privacy and security success criteria
sections.guidance: Turn privacy and security expectations into observable conditions the gates can test: classification, de-identification, small-count suppression, RLS, the privacy impact assessment, access controls and a restore test. Cite the Health Information Act duties by section only where the duty is certain. Good: the go-live gate can tick each line on evidence.

sections.heading: Key risks, assumptions and constraints
sections.guidance: Summarize the main risks with RAID IDs and owners, the assumptions you are relying on, and the fixed constraints (dates, money, law, contracts, calendar). Keep each to one line. Good: the sponsor can see what she is accepting by signing.

sections.heading: Approval
sections.guidance: Record who approved, on what date, with the decision ID, and list any later versions with what changed. Good: an auditor can tell which version was authorized and that later edits did not change scope, budget or dates without a decision.

## Purpose and justification

Project Beacon gives Kestrel Health Network (KHN) trusted patient-flow analytics, safe clinician access and proven recovery from cyber attack, each run as a supported service, at Kestrel General Hospital (KGH), Aspen Ridge Hospital, Coulee Valley Hospital and Prairie Gate Health Centre (PGH). The business case (BCN-R1-03) holds the evidence.

## Objectives and success measures

By 2026-12-17 Beacon will:

1. Replace emailed Excel extracts with de-identified Power BI dashboards for emergency department (ED) flow and bed occupancy at all four sites.
2. Drive clinician access from human resources (HR) events and roles, with multi-factor authentication (MFA), single sign-on, privileged access control and quarterly access reviews.
3. Set and test recovery targets for clinical systems, first the Clinical Information System (CIS), and prepare ransomware response.

Measured three months after each gate (Release 1 measures on 2027-01-25, Release 2 measures on 2027-02-26, Release 3 and programme measures on 2027-03-17):

| Measure | Baseline (data) | Target (agreed) | Owner |
|---|---|---|---|
| Median minutes, arrival to physician initial assessment (PIA), KGH | 80.5 | 60 | Dr. Sarah Whitford (E-007) |
| Left without being seen (LWBS) rate, all sites | 5.7% | 4.5% | Dr. Sarah Whitford (E-007) |
| Access requests resolved within 72 hours | 27.3% | 80% | Grace Liu (E-005) |
| Median days to fulfil an access request | 4.26 | 1 | Grace Liu (E-005) |
| Missed leavers | 2 | 0 | Nora Lindqvist (E-018) |
| Privileged accounts with MFA | 66.7% | 100% | Daniel Osei (E-004) |
| Q3 access reviews completed on time | 66.7% | 100% | Daniel Osei (E-004) |
| CIS restore within its 4-hour recovery time objective (RTO) | Failed (9.0 h and 13.5 h; last test 2025-08-14) | Pass | Daniel Osei (E-004) |
| Security awareness, agency and vendor workers | 48% | 90% | Daniel Osei (E-004) |

## High-level scope

- Release 1: patient-flow analytics service for all four sites.
- Release 2: role-based access, joiner-mover-leaver from HR, MFA and single sign-on, privileged access, access reviews, access requests via the service desk.
- Release 3: business impact analysis, recovery targets, CIS restore and downtime tests, incident response, vulnerability remediation, a security-operations dashboard.
- Out of scope: replacing any clinical system; patient names or other identifying details on dashboards; real-time reporting; non-clinical applications.

## Milestones and budget

| Milestone | Date | Decided by |
|---|---|---|
| Charter approved (D-01) | 2026-09-01 | Sponsor |
| Release 1 go-live gate | 2026-10-23 | Sponsor, on the Programme Manager's recommendation, after the business owners (E-007, E-008) and the service owner (E-005) accept |
| Release 2 acceptance gate | 2026-11-26 | Sponsor and Chief Information Security Officer |
| Programme acceptance | 2026-12-17 | Sponsor |

Budget at completion: CAD (Canadian dollars) 1,200,000 across 15 work packages (Release 1 CAD 420,000; Release 2 CAD 460,000; Release 3 CAD 320,000). Management reserve: CAD 120,000, held by the sponsor outside the register. Total authorized: CAD 1,320,000.

## Governance and authority

- Sponsor, Dr. Helen Marchetti (E-001): decides gates, releases management reserve, accepts residual risk on the advice of Daniel Osei (E-004), Chief Information Security Officer.
- Change-control board (CCB), chaired by Marcus Bell (E-002), Chief Information Officer: decides changes to scope, baseline dates and budget under the change-control process (BCN-R1-12). A change that moves a gate or uses the reserve goes through the board to the sponsor for decision.
- Priya Raman (E-003) approves the privacy impact assessment. Grace Liu (E-005) accepts each service into support. Data owners: Dr. Sarah Whitford (E-007) for emergency data, Janelle Cardinal (E-008) for bed data; Tomás Rivera (E-006) is data steward.
- The Programme Manager directs the team and vendors within approved scope, re-sequences work inside float, spends within each work-package budget and manages issues. Anything that moves a gate, the budget at completion or the reserve goes to the CCB.

## Privacy and security success criteria

- No individually identifying health information in the semantic model; dashboards labelled Confidential.
- Counts under 5 suppressed, and rates whose numerator is under 5 blanked, in any report shared outside the care team (Kestrel rule), tested before go-live.
- Each site role sees only its own rows, proven by positive and negative row-level security tests.
- The privacy impact assessment is approved by Priya Raman and submitted to the Information and Privacy Commissioner for review and comment before Release 1 goes live (Health Information Act, section 64).
- Release 2: no missed leavers, MFA on every privileged account, and nobody holding two or more of provision accounts, approve access and administer audit logs on the Identity Directory (A-007).
- Release 3: a CIS restore test passes its 4-hour RTO and the incident response plan is exercised.

## Key risks, assumptions and constraints

- Risks (RAID log BCN-R1-11): R-01 ED data quality (E-006); R-02 PGH small counts (E-003); R-03 MFA at shared workstations (E-008); R-04 CIS restore (E-004); R-05 security logs processed in the United States (E-003); R-06 key-person dependency and R-07 Lumen contract end (Programme Manager); R-08 cost (E-002).
- Assumptions: source extracts keep flowing; named staff are available as scheduled; Meridian Clinical Systems (V-01) supports the CIS restore.
- Constraints: finish 2026-12-17; CAD 1,320,000 authorized; Health Information Act sections 57, 58 and 60; Lumen Analytics Partners (V-05) contract ends 2026-11-30; Monday to Friday calendar.

## Approval

Approved by Dr. Helen Marchetti, executive sponsor, on 2026-09-01 (D-01). Version 1.1 (2026-10-01) replaced provisional baselines with Q3 2026 data; no scope, budget or date changed, so no change request was needed.
mistakes: Writing a project plan instead of a charter. The charter authorizes and sets boundaries; detailed requirements, the WBS and the schedule come after it.
Leaving the Programme Manager's authority vague. Say what you may decide alone and what must go to the change-control board or the sponsor.
Success measures without baselines, owners or a measurement date. Each needs all four, or nobody can say at closure whether Beacon worked.
Treating privacy and security as a later workstream. The criteria belong in the charter so the go-live gate can test them, as D-02 did with small-count suppression.

items.purpose: The scope statement defines exactly what Release 1 delivers, what it does not, the constraints and assumptions, and how each deliverable is accepted. You write it in week 2, day 2 from the charter and the requirements register. Dr. Helen Marchetti approves it, and the data owners, Dr. Sarah Whitford and Janelle Cardinal, agree the acceptance criteria. The team builds to it, the change-control board uses it to tell a change from a clarification, and the go-live gate on 2026-10-23 checks against it. With the WBS and WBS dictionary it forms the scope baseline.

sections.heading: Product scope description
sections.guidance: Describe the product itself: what data goes in, where it is processed, what users get and how it is secured and supported. Name the systems with their asset IDs and the Power BI choices that shape the build, such as storage mode, refresh, RLS and the sensitivity label. Good: a new analyst could sketch the data flow from this paragraph alone.

sections.heading: Deliverables
sections.guidance: List each thing the release hands over, with an ID and the work package that produces it. Deliverables are nouns you can inspect, not activities. Good: every deliverable maps to exactly one work package in the WBS, and nothing in the WBS is missing from the list.

sections.heading: Acceptance criteria
sections.guidance: For each area (data, measures, access, privacy, quality, service) write a pass or fail test and the evidence that proves it. Use the approved reconciliation numbers wherever a measure is involved, so accuracy is a number, not an opinion. Good: two people checking the same evidence would reach the same verdict.

sections.heading: Exclusions
sections.guidance: Say plainly what Release 1 will not do, especially anything a stakeholder has hinted at wanting. An exclusion written down turns a later request into a change request instead of an argument. Good: the list covers patient-level data, source-system changes, real-time reporting and work belonging to later releases.

sections.heading: Constraints
sections.guidance: List the fixed limits: the gate date, the release budget, the Health Information Act duties, Kestrel policy, contracts and the calendar. A constraint is not up for negotiation by the team. Good: each one is specific (a date, an amount, a section number or a policy rule).

sections.heading: Assumptions
sections.guidance: List what you believe is true but have not proved, each with who confirms it. Assumptions that turn out false become risks or issues, so they also go in the RAID log. Good: each is testable and owned.

sections.heading: Acceptance process and sign-off
sections.guidance: Set out the steps from evidence to decision: who tests, who accepts the service into support, who decides at the gate and how changes to the scope are handled. Good: the process uses the schedule's task numbers and dates, so nobody wonders when acceptance happens.

## Product scope description

Release 1 delivers the patient-flow analytics service for Kestrel General Hospital (KGH), Aspen Ridge Hospital (ARH), Coulee Valley Hospital (CVH) and Prairie Gate Health Centre (PGH). Visit times from the Emergency Department Tracking Board (A-002) and the bed census from the Bed Management System (A-006) land in the Clinical Data Warehouse (A-010), where de-identified views are built. The Power BI semantic model (A-009) loads those views in Import storage mode, refreshes daily at 05:00 through the on-premises data gateway so pages show yesterday's data by 06:00, filters rows by site with row-level security (RLS) and carries the Confidential sensitivity label. Users get the reports as a Power BI app, and the IT service desk supports them. The emailed Excel extracts stop once the service is live.

## Deliverables

| ID | Deliverable | Work package |
|---|---|---|
| DEL-01 | Profiled and cleaned emergency department (ED), bed census and service desk data, with an exception table for quarantined rows | WP-103 |
| DEL-02 | De-identified warehouse views | WP-103 |
| DEL-03 | Semantic model: star schema, marked date table, documented DAX (Data Analysis Expressions) measures | WP-104 |
| DEL-04 | Executive and site operations report pages, published as an app | WP-104 |
| DEL-05 | RLS roles, sensitivity label and RLS test pack | WP-104 |
| DEL-06 | Classification register, privacy impact assessment and threat model | WP-102 |
| DEL-07 | Service catalogue entry, knowledge articles and support handover | WP-105 |

## Acceptance criteria

Each criterion is pass or fail against the approved Q3 2026 reconciliation (1 July to 30 September 2026).

| Area | Criterion | Evidence |
|---|---|---|
| Data | 480 ED source rows give 474 valid visits: 2 exact duplicates removed, 4 rows quarantined with their rule IDs, none deleted | Data-quality workbook |
| ED measures | All sites: median 64.0 minutes to physician initial assessment (PIA) over 445 visits; left without being seen (LWBS) 5.7%; 28.3% within the Canadian Triage and Acuity Scale (CTAS) objective. KGH: 80.5 minutes, LWBS 7.5% | DAX catalogue tests |
| Bed measures | Average daily occupancy 87.0%; 121 of 144 staffed beds (84.0%) on 2026-09-30; beds never added across days | DAX catalogue tests |
| Access | Each site role sees only its own rows; the all-sites role sees four sites; a user in no role sees no data; consumers are app Viewers, where RLS applies | RLS test pack |
| Privacy | No direct identifiers in the model; counts under 5 suppressed, and rates whose numerator is under 5 blanked, in pages shared outside the care team | RLS test pack; privacy impact assessment |
| Quality | Accessibility checks pass at the level set in the quality plan; every visual renders in 3 seconds or less in Performance Analyzer (agreed) | Quality plan results |
| Service | The 05:00 scheduled refresh succeeds and shows yesterday's data by 06:00 on every user acceptance testing (UAT) day, 2026-10-21 to 2026-10-23; the desk logs and routes a test incident with the knowledge articles | Refresh history; handover record |

## Exclusions

- Patient names, health numbers, dates of birth or bed numbers, on any page or in the model.
- Changes to the source systems or to the Clinical Information System (CIS).
- DirectQuery or real-time pages; Release 1 uses scheduled Import refresh.
- Forecasting models of ED demand.
- Release 2 access work and Release 3 resilience work.

## Constraints

- Release 1 go-live gate 2026-10-23. Release 1 budget CAD (Canadian dollars) 420,000, WP-101 to WP-105.
- Health Information Act: highest degree of anonymity and only the information essential to the purpose (sections 57 and 58); safeguards (section 60); a privacy impact assessment submitted to the Information and Privacy Commissioner for review and comment before implementation (section 64).
- Kestrel policy: dashboards classified Confidential; counts under 5 suppressed, and rates whose numerator is under 5 blanked, outside the care team.
- Lumen Analytics Partners (V-05) works on a fixed-price contract that ends 2026-11-30.
- Schedule calendar: Monday to Friday, no holidays.

## Assumptions

- Daily extracts from A-002 and A-006 keep reaching A-010. Confirms: Tomás Rivera (E-006).
- The on-premises data gateway can reach A-010 for scheduled refresh. Confirms: Tomás Rivera.
- Dr. Sarah Whitford, Janelle Cardinal and Mei Tanaka (E-013) are free for UAT, 2026-10-21 to 2026-10-23. Confirms: Programme Manager.
- Tomás Rivera stays available for critical tasks 6, 8 and 9 (risk R-06).

## Acceptance process and sign-off

1. The build team files evidence against every criterion before UAT starts.
2. UAT runs as schedule task 11 with the Emergency Medical Director, the Director of Patient Flow and the Clinical Analyst. Each failed criterion becomes a defect with an owner.
3. Dr. Sarah Whitford (E-007) and Janelle Cardinal (E-008) accept the business criteria, and Grace Liu (E-005) accepts the service into support.
4. The Programme Manager recommends, and Dr. Helen Marchetti (E-001) decides at the go-live gate (task 12) on 2026-10-23. Priya Raman (E-003) verifies any privacy condition attached to the decision.

Changes to this statement go to the change-control board under BCN-R1-12. A request for anything under Exclusions is a change, not a clarification.
mistakes: Acceptance criteria nobody can test, such as accurate dashboards. Give the numbers the model must reproduce: 474 valid visits, 64.0 minutes, 87.0% occupancy.

Leaving out exclusions. Unwritten exclusions become scope creep. Writing down 'no patient-level lists' early is what later lets the change-control board treat a request such as CR-01 as a change, not a clarification.
Mixing up constraints and assumptions. The 2026-10-23 gate is a constraint; gateway connectivity is an assumption you must check.
Letting the build team accept its own work. The data owners and the service owner accept, on evidence, and the sponsor decides at the gate.

items.purpose: The requirements and traceability register records what the emergency and patient-flow leaders, privacy, security and support need, turns each need into a testable requirement, and traces it back to its source and forward to design, build, test and acceptance. You open it in week 2, day 1 after elicitation and complete the traceability in week 2, day 2. Dr. Sarah Whitford and Janelle Cardinal approve the requirements. Tomás Rivera's team builds and tests from it, and the change-control board uses it to see exactly what a change touches.

sections.heading: Elicitation summary
sections.guidance: Record who you spoke to, how (interviews, workshops, observation, document analysis) and the main things you learned. Include frontline users, not just leaders. Good: a reviewer can see every source of every requirement, and the findings point at real evidence such as the extracts and the Q3 data.

sections.heading: Writing rules and priorities
sections.guidance: State the rules every requirement follows: one need per line, a named source, a MoSCoW priority and a pass or fail acceptance criterion. Show one worked example of a vague need becoming a requirement. Good: two analysts would write the same requirement from the same interview note.

sections.heading: Requirements register
sections.guidance: One row per requirement: ID, requirement, source, priority, acceptance criterion and status. Use the approved reconciliation figures as acceptance values so accuracy is testable. Include privacy, security, support and accessibility requirements, not only measures. Keep rejected requests in the register with the decision that closed them.

sections.heading: Traceability matrix
sections.guidance: Trace each requirement forward to the design document, the work package and schedule task that build it, and the test that proves it. Good: from any test you can find the requirement it proves, and from any requirement the evidence that it is met. A requirement with no test is not finished.

sections.heading: Open data questions
sections.guidance: List the questions only a data owner can answer, with the owner and status. These come from profiling and must not be fixed by guesswork. Good: each question names the exact rows and the person who decides.

sections.heading: Change history
sections.guidance: Record each version with its date and what changed, and link every change to the decision that allowed it. Good: an auditor can see why REQ-13 was refused and what replaced it, without asking anyone.

items.purpose: The work breakdown structure (WBS) breaks Project Beacon into its three releases and then into 15 work packages, each with one owner, a budget, dates and outputs you can test. Its dictionary says what each package contains, so nothing is done twice or missed. You build it in week 2, day 3, before the schedule, because every schedule task must belong to a work package. Dr. Helen Marchetti approves it as part of the scope baseline. Package owners plan from it, finance uses it as the cost structure, and the earned value report rolls up through it.

sections.heading: Structure
sections.guidance: Show the hierarchy from the programme to the releases to the work packages, with a WBS code and budget at each level. Decompose by deliverable, not by department. Good: the tree fits on one screen and each release is clearly separate.

sections.heading: WBS dictionary
sections.guidance: For each work package give the WBS code, ID and name, owner, budget, dates and main outputs. A package with no owner is a gap you must flag, not hide. Good: an owner can read their row and know what done looks like.

sections.heading: Budget roll-up and 100% check
sections.guidance: Add the packages up to the releases and the releases up to the budget at completion, then show the management reserve separately. Apply the 100% rule: the children add up exactly to the parent, and all of the work is in the tree once. Good: the totals match the charter to the dollar.

sections.heading: Link to the schedule
sections.guidance: Map every schedule task to its work package so cost and time roll up the same way. Keep milestones at release level. Good: no schedule task is orphaned and no package lacks a task.

sections.heading: Register corrections
sections.guidance: If the work package register came with errors, list each finding, the data-quality rule and the correction, with who confirmed it. Show the wrong totals you avoided. Good: anyone can rebuild the CAD 1,200,000 total from the raw file by following these lines.

sections.heading: Status and change control
sections.guidance: Give each package's status on the status date and explain how earned value is taken per package. Say what kind of change needs the change-control board. Good: the earned value figures agree with the status report exactly.

items.purpose: The Microsoft Project schedule sequences every Beacon task, shows the dependencies and the critical path, and fixes the dates of the three gates. sections.heading: Schedule set-up
sections.guidance: Record the source file, project start date, calendar, link type, field mapping and how the summary row was built. These choices change every date, so write them down. sections.heading: Milestones and gates
sections.guidance: List each milestone with its ID, date, the people in its resource column and who decides it. Good: the dates and the decision makers match the charter exactly.

sections.heading: Task schedule
sections.guidance: Show every task with duration, early start, early finish and total float from the forward and backward pass. Good: each row matches the approved schedule figures, and the reader knows the dates are early dates.

sections.heading: Critical path
sections.guidance: List the critical path by task ID, then in words, and say what drives it at each step. Explain how to show it in Microsoft Project. Good: the reader knows which tasks move the programme end day for day.

sections.heading: Float and near-critical work
sections.guidance: List every task with float, giving total float and free float, and explain the difference between the two kinds of float. Name near-critical tasks. Good: the reader can see which slips are harmless and which quietly push another task.

sections.heading: Resources and over-allocation
sections.guidance: Check who is booked on overlapping tasks, especially on the critical path, and say what you will do about it. Link findings to the RAID log. Good: over-allocations are found here, before they turn into missed dates.

sections.heading: Status, calendar and baseline control
sections.guidance: Report progress at the status date, test the calendar assumption, and state the rules for changing the baseline. Good: the effect of any holiday or late task on the gates is given in dates, not adjectives.

items.purpose: The stakeholder register lists everyone who affects or is affected by Beacon: what they care about, how much power and interest they have, how engaged they are now, how engaged you need them to be, and what you will do about the gap. You build it in week 2, day 4 and review it every two weeks and at each gate. You own it, and the sponsor reviews it. Because it holds frank assessments of named people it is classified Confidential and not circulated. You use it to write the communication plan, choose UAT and pilot testers, and prepare for every change-control decision.

sections.heading: Stakeholder identification
sections.guidance: List every person, group and organization with a stake: leaders, frontline users, privacy, security, support, HR, vendors, the regulator and patients. For each, give the ID, role, main interest or concern and a power and interest rating. Tie concerns to evidence such as a risk ID or a baseline figure. Good: nobody who could stop or slow Beacon is missing.

sections.heading: Power and interest analysis
sections.guidance: Place each stakeholder in a quadrant: manage closely, keep satisfied, keep informed, or monitor. This tells you how much effort each relationship needs. Good: the people in manage closely are the ones who decide gates and own data.

sections.heading: Engagement assessment
sections.guidance: For the stakeholders who matter most, record current and desired engagement (unaware, resistant, neutral, supportive, leading), the action that closes the gap and who owns it. Be honest about resistance. Good: every gap has one concrete action with an owner.

sections.heading: Service relationships
sections.guidance: Describe the analytics service as a relationship between consumers, the provider, and partners and suppliers, and say how value is co-created. This is where ITIL meets stakeholder management. Good: it is clear who defines the outcome, who runs the service and who supplies parts of it.

sections.heading: Review and change log
sections.guidance: State how often the register is reviewed and record each version with what changed and why. Stakeholders change as releases change, so the log shows the register is alive. Good: new stakeholders appear when the work that affects them begins.

items.purpose: The communication plan sets out who needs what information about Beacon, when, in what form, through which channel and from whom, and how you will know it worked. You build it in week 2, day 4 straight from the stakeholder register. You own it and the sponsor agrees it. The team, the service desk and each message owner use it every week. Review it at every release, because Release 2 (MFA and new access routes) and Release 3 (downtime procedures) bring new audiences.

sections.heading: Goals and principles
sections.guidance: State what communication must achieve and the few rules everyone follows: who hears first, where the single source of truth lives, and when to meet rather than email. Good: the rules settle most what-should-I-send questions without asking you.

sections.heading: Audiences and needs
sections.guidance: Group the stakeholder register into audiences and say what each needs to know. Write needs, not channels. Good: each audience maps back to register entries, and the needs differ in depth and timing.

sections.heading: Communication matrix
sections.guidance: One row per communication: what, audience, owner, method (interactive, push or pull) and when. Use real dates from the schedule where an event drives the message. Good: every row has a single owner and a cadence or trigger.

sections.heading: Status reporting
sections.guidance: Define the standard status report: its sections, its earned value figures, and the rules that set red, amber and green. Show one worked example. Good: two people applying the rules to the same data give the same colour.

sections.heading: Escalation and urgent messages
sections.guidance: Set the routes for issues, privacy breaches, security incidents and gate decisions, with time limits. Use the Health Information Act breach duty exactly as written. Good: a service desk analyst knows whom to call within minutes of a suspected breach.

sections.heading: Handling sensitive information
sections.guidance: Say what must never appear in a message and how documents are classified. Separate patient health information from staff personal information, because different laws apply. Good: no status report or slide could ever expose a patient.

sections.heading: Measuring effectiveness
sections.guidance: Say how you will know messages landed: closed actions, what testers can explain, and the questions the service desk receives. Good: at least one measure catches a missed message within days, not months.

## Goals and principles

- Decision makers hear news before frontline staff, and nobody learns of a change from a dashboard.
- One source of truth: the Beacon document library, the RAID (risks, assumptions, issues and decisions) log and the dashboards, not email attachments.
- Meet to decide (interactive), send to record (push), publish for reference (pull).
- Beacon has 20 named people, counting the Programme Manager, so there are 190 possible two-way channels (n(n-1)/2 = 20 x 19 / 2). Messages go through named owners, not everyone to everyone.

## Audiences and needs

| Audience | Needs to know |

| Sponsor and change-control board (CCB) | Progress to the gates, cost, decisions needed, top risks |
| Privacy and security (E-003, E-004, E-020) | Data flows, classification, test evidence, anything leaving Alberta |
| Data owners and users (E-007, E-008, E-010, E-012) | Definitions, what changes on go-live day, how to give feedback |

| Human resources (HR) and vendors (E-018, V-01, V-03, V-04) | Their actions and deadlines in Releases 2 and 3 |
| Information and Privacy Commissioner | The privacy impact assessment, before go-live |

## Communication matrix

| Communication | Audience | Owner | Method | When |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Sponsor check-in | E-001 | Programme Manager | Meeting (interactive) | Weekly, Monday |
| Status report | E-001 to E-005 | Programme Manager | Report in the library, email notice (push) | Weekly, Friday |
| Change-control board | CCB members | Marcus Bell (E-002) | Meeting; decisions into the RAID log | Every two weeks and on demand |
| Release 1 working group | E-006, E-007, E-008, E-013 | Tomás Rivera | Meeting with a live model demo | Weekly during build |
| Data-quality exceptions | E-007, E-008 | Tomás Rivera | Exception list from the workbook (push) | When a refresh quarantines rows |
| Privacy and security review | E-003, E-004 | Programme Manager | Workshop | Before each gate |
| Service desk briefing | E-005 and analysts | Grace Liu | Briefing and knowledge articles | Task 10, 2026-10-16 to 2026-10-21 |
| Go-live notice | Dashboard users at all four sites | Janelle Cardinal | Email and huddle script | After the gate on 2026-10-23 |
| Vendor check-in | V-01, V-04, V-05 | Programme Manager | Meeting | Every two weeks |
| Programme news | All Kestrel staff | Dr. Helen Marchetti | Intranet article (pull) | At each gate |

## Status reporting

One page, every Friday:

1. Overall status for cost and schedule, using the rules below.
2. Gates (2026-10-23, 2026-11-26, 2026-12-17) with the current forecast.
3. Earned value: planned value, earned value, actual cost, cost performance index (CPI), schedule performance index (SPI), estimate at completion.
4. Top five risks and open issues from the RAID log.
5. Decisions needed, from whom, by when.

Rules (agreed): Red when a gate is forecast to slip or the estimate at completion exceeds total authorized funding; Amber when CPI or SPI is below 1.0 without a Red condition; otherwise Green.

Example for 2026-10-01: Cost is Red, because the estimate at completion (CAD 1,342,500) exceeds the CAD 1,320,000 authorized. Schedule is Amber at SPI 0.80 while the WP-102 and WP-103 owners confirm the gate forecast.

## Escalation and urgent messages

- An issue the team cannot resolve in 2 working days goes to the Programme Manager, then the sponsor (agreed).
- Suspected privacy breach: tell Priya Raman (E-003) at once. Affiliates must report to Kestrel as custodian. Where there is a risk of harm, Kestrel must notify the Information and Privacy Commissioner as soon as practicable, and also the Minister responsible under the Act and the affected individuals (Health Information Act, section 60.1).
- Security incident: service desk to Sam Okafor (E-020), then Daniel Osei (E-004).
- Gate decisions go to every audience within one working day (agreed).

## Handling sensitive information

- No patient-level data in email, status reports or slides. Use the Confidential dashboards, with counts under 5 suppressed, and rates whose numerator is under 5 blanked, outside the care team.
- Status reports are Internal. The stakeholder register is Confidential and goes to the sponsor only.
- Staff matters such as I-01 are handled one to one. Staff personal information falls under the Protection of Privacy Act, not the Health Information Act.

## Measuring effectiveness

- Meeting actions closed by their due date, tracked in the RAID log.
- At user acceptance testing, every tester can say what changes on go-live day.
- After go-live, service desk calls asking for the old extract signal a missed message.
- The plan is reviewed at each gate. Release 2 adds clinicians and agency nurses as audiences for MFA (multi-factor authentication) and new request routes.
mistakes: Sending one message to everyone. A charge nurse and the Chief Information Officer need different content, depth and timing.
Planning only push communication. Email informs but agrees nothing; decisions need interactive meetings.
Putting patient detail in status emails or slides. Point to the Confidential dashboards and apply the under-5 suppression rule.
Never checking whether it worked. Calls asking for the old extract after go-live show a message was missed.

items.purpose: The RAID log is Beacon's single register of risks, assumptions, issues and decisions. Each entry has an ID, an owner, a response or action, dates and a status, so nothing important lives only in someone's inbox. You open it in week 2, day 5 and keep it for the whole programme; Releases 2 and 3 add to it. You maintain it, owners update their own entries, and the sponsor and change-control board review it at every meeting. At closure, open risks pass to the residual risk register and the decisions section becomes the record of who decided what.

sections.heading: Scoring and review rules
sections.guidance: Set the probability and impact scale, how to write a risk, the allowed responses and the review cadence. Say how a risk becomes an issue. Good: two people scoring the same risk land on the same rating, and everyone knows when the log is reviewed.

sections.heading: Risks
sections.guidance: Write each risk as cause, event and effect, with probability and impact, a response strategy and actions, one owner, and a trigger and status. Use the evidence behind each risk. Good: the response attacks the cause, the trigger is observable, and every Beacon risk ID is present.

sections.heading: Assumptions
sections.guidance: List what the plan relies on but has not proved, with an owner, when it will be checked and its status. Close an assumption once proved, or convert it to a risk or issue if it fails. Good: each one has a check date.

sections.heading: Issues
sections.guidance: Record problems that have already happened: what happened, the owner, actions, due date and status. Separate containment (stop the harm now) from the permanent fix. Good: each issue has a date and an owner who can act.

sections.heading: Decisions
sections.guidance: Record each significant decision with ID, date, what was decided, who decided and its effect, including the reasoning when a request is refused. Good: an auditor can follow every baseline change back to a decision.

sections.heading: Escalation and closure
sections.guidance: Say what goes to the sponsor and how fast, how entries close, and where open risks go at programme closure. Good: nothing is deleted, and nothing stays open without an owner after Beacon ends.
